claim: Eight neurologically healthy volunteers participated in the experiment (six male, aged 28.5 ± 8.52 years).
source: Eight neurologically healthy volunteers participated in the experiment (six male, aged 28.5 ± 8.52 years).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number, sex distribution, and age of participants.

claim: The study protocol was approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (reference number 5833/001).
source: The study protocol, participant information, and form of consent, were approved by the UCL Research Ethics Committee (reference number 5833/001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethics approval details.

claim: In most trials (70%), the direction of coherent motion in the RDK was congruent to the direction of the instruction cue.
source: Participants were instructed that in most of the trials (70%), the direction of coherent motion in the RDK was congruent to the direction of the instruction cue.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design parameter.

claim: Accuracy increased with increasing coherence in congruent trials.
source: Accuracy increased with increasing coherence in congruent trials, and worsened with increasing coherence in incongruent trials.
evidence: The manuscript text states this finding and Figure 1C shows the data supporting this claim.

claim: There was a significant interaction between congruence and coherence for accuracy (χ2(2) = 363.21, p<0.001).
source: This was demonstrated by a significant interaction between congruence and coherence for accuracy (χ2(2) = 363.21, p<0.001), and RT (F(2,16187) = 25.83, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Response times were faster during congruent trials than incongruent trials at all coherence levels.
source: Pairwise comparisons (Tukey corrected) showed that accuracy was higher and RTs were faster during congruent trials than incongruent trials at low (accuracy: Z = 7.83, p<0.001; RT: t(16181.94) = −8.25, p<0.0001), medium (accuracy: Z = 23.71, p<0.001; RT: t(16181.94) = −13.94, p<0.001) and high coherence levels (accuracy: Z = 29.96, p<0.001; RT: t(16181.94) = −18.39, p<0.001).
evidence: The manuscript provides detailed statistical comparisons of response times across conditions.

claim: Within-session movement was <0.2 mm in the x and y dimensions, and <1.5 mm in the z dimension.
source: In all participants, within-session movement was <0.2 mm in the x and y dimensions, and <1.5 mm in the z dimension, while co-registration error was <1.5 mm in any dimension (estimated by calculating the within-participant standard deviation of the absolute coil locations across recording blocks; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states the movement measurements and references a figure showing the data.

claim: Co-registration error was <1.5 mm in any dimension.
source: In all participants, within-session movement was <0.2 mm in the x and y dimensions, and <1.5 mm in the z dimension, while co-registration error was <1.5 mm in any dimension (estimated by calculating the within-participant standard deviation of the absolute coil locations across recording blocks; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the co-registration error measurements.

claim: The intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) was greater than 0.9 for all task epochs for the participant shown in Figure 2.
source: For the participant shown in Figure 2, the intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), a measure of test-retest reliability, was greater than 0.9 for all task epochs, and the three measures used to assess reproducibility
evidence: The manuscript provides ICC values as a measure of data reproducibility.

claim: Across all subjects, the mean ICC for all task epochs and reproducibility measures was greater than 0.85.
source: Across all subjects, the mean ICC for all task epochs and reproducibility measures was greater than 0.85
evidence: The manuscript provides summary statistics of ICC across all participants.

claim: Attention to visual stimuli is associated with decreases in alpha and increases in gamma activity in visual cortex.
source: Attention to visual stimuli is associated with decreases in alpha (Hari, 1997; Sauseng et al., 2005; Yamagishi et al., 2005; Thut et al., 2006; Mazaheri et al., 2014) and increases in gamma activity in visual cortex (Müller et al., 1996; Fries et al., 2001; Busch et al., 2004; Hoogenboom et al., 2006; Muthukumaraswamy and Singh, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established finding.

claim: Sensors overlying the visual cortex revealed a significant decrease in alpha (7–13 Hz) and increase in gamma (60 – 90 Hz) power following the onset of the RDK.
source: In line with previous research, sensors overlying the visual cortex revealed a significant decrease in alpha (7–13 Hz) and increase in gamma (60 – 90 Hz) power following the onset of the RDK and lasting for its duration (Siegel et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and Figure 3A shows the time-frequency data.

claim: There was a burst of gamma activity following the onset of the instruction cue.
source: In addition, we observed a burst of gamma activity following the onset of the instruction cue (Figure 3A; significant time-frequency windows marked, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: The manuscript describes this observation and references Figure 3A showing the data.

claim: Motor responses are associated with a decrease in beta power prior to movement, followed by a rebound in beta activity after the response.
source: Motor responses are associated with a characteristic pattern of spectral activity in contralateral sensorimotor cortex, with a stereotypical decrease in average beta power prior to movement, followed by a rebound in average beta activity after the response.
evidence: The manuscript describes established patterns of motor-related brain activity.

claim: A burst of gamma activity typically occurs around movement onset.
source: Moreover, a burst of gamma activity typically occurs around movement onset (Pfurtscheller et al., 1996; Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 1997; Crone et al., 1998; Cheyne et al., 2008; Huo et al., 2010; Gaetz et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established finding.

claim: A significant decrease in beta power (15 – 30 Hz) was observed prior to and during the participant's response along with a subsequent rebound.
source: At the sensor-level, we indeed observed these classic average power changes, with a significant decrease in beta power (15 – 30 Hz) prior to and during the participant's response along with a subsequent rebound, and a burst of response-aligned gamma (60 – 90 Hz) activity (Figure 3B; significant time-frequency windows marked, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observed beta power changes and references Figure 3B.

claim: A burst of response-aligned gamma (60 – 90 Hz) activity was observed.
source: At the sensor-level, we indeed observed these classic average power changes, with a significant decrease in beta power (15 – 30 Hz) prior to and during the participant's response along with a subsequent rebound, and a burst of response-aligned gamma (60 – 90 Hz) activity (Figure 3B; significant time-frequency windows marked, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: The manuscript describes the observed gamma activity and references Figure 3B.

claim: Low frequency activity (alpha, 7 – 13 Hz; and beta, 15 – 30 Hz) predominately originated from deep cortical laminae.
source: We found that low frequency activity (alpha, 7 – 13 Hz; and beta, 15 – 30 Hz) predominately originated from deep cortical laminae, and high frequency activity (gamma, 60 – 90 Hz) from more superficial laminae in both visual and sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main finding of the study.

claim: High frequency activity (gamma, 60 – 90 Hz) originated from more superficial laminae in both visual and sensorimotor cortex.
source: We found that low frequency activity (alpha, 7 – 13 Hz; and beta, 15 – 30 Hz) predominately originated from deep cortical laminae, and high frequency activity (gamma, 60 – 90 Hz) from more superficial laminae in both visual and sensorimotor cortex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this main finding of the study.

claim: Visual alpha activity of most participants was classified as originating from the white matter surface (global: W(8)=0, p=0.008, 8/8 participants).
source: When averaging the change in power either over the whole brain, within a functionally-defined ROI, or an anatomically constrained ROI, the visual alpha activity of most participants was classified as originating from the white matter surface (global: W(8)=0, p=0.008, 8/8 participants, functional ROI: W(8)=2, p=0.023, 7/8 participants, anatomical ROI: W(8)=16, p=0.844, 5/8 participants; Figure 5A, right).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 5A.

claim: Visual gamma was strongest on the pial surface for RDK-aligned gamma (global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants).
source: This was consistently observed for the global, functional, and anatomical ROI metrics (RDK gamma, global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; RDK gamma, functional ROI: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; RDK gamma, anatomical ROI: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; instruction cue gamma, global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; instruction cue gamma, functional ROI: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; instruction cue gamma, anatomical ROI: W(8)=28, p=0.195, 5/8 participants).
evidence: The manuscript provides detailed statistical results for visual gamma localization.

claim: Sensorimotor beta decrease localized to the white matter surface (global: W(8)=0, p=0.008).
source: This result held for all but one participant at the single participant level, and overall at the group level (beta decrease, global: W(8)=0, p=0.008; beta decrease, functional ROI: W(8)=6, p=0.109; beta decrease, anatomical ROI: W(8)=0, p=0.008; beta rebound, global: W(8)=1, p=0.016; beta rebound, functional ROI: W(8)=2, p=0.023; beta rebound, anatomical ROI: W(8)=0, p=0.008).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results for sensorimotor beta localization.

claim: Sensorimotor beta rebound localized to the white matter surface (global: W(8)=1, p=0.016).
source: This result held for all but one participant at the single participant level, and overall at the group level (beta decrease, global: W(8)=0, p=0.008; beta decrease, functional ROI: W(8)=6, p=0.109; beta decrease, anatomical ROI: W(8)=0, p=0.008; beta rebound, global: W(8)=1, p=0.016; beta rebound, functional ROI: W(8)=2, p=0.023; beta rebound, anatomical ROI: W(8)=0, p=0.008).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results for sensorimotor beta rebound localization.

claim: Movement-related gamma localized to the pial surface (global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants).
source: Turning to the burst of gamma aligned with the onset of the movement and localized to the same patch of left sensorimotor cortex (Figure 6C), we found that this signal was strongest on the pial surface (global: W(8)=35, p=0.016, 7/8 participants; functional ROI: W(8)=33, p=0.039, 6/8 participants; anatomical ROI: W(8)=31, p=0.078, 6/8 participants).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical results and references Figure 6C.

claim: Shuffling the position of the sensors resulted in all signals localizing to the pial surface.
source: Shuffling the position of the sensors destroys any correspondence between the anatomy and the sensor data. Added co-registration error simulates the effect of between-session spatial uncertainty arising from head movement and inaccuracies of the forward model typically experienced without head-casts (Uutela et al., 2001; Hillebrand and Barnes, 2003; Hillebrand and Barnes, 2011; Medvedovsky et al., 2007; Troebinger et al., 2014a; Meyer et al., 2017b). For both control analyses, all signals now localized to the pial surface (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), suggesting that the laminar discrimination between low- and high-frequency signals in our main analyses relies on precise anatomical models.
evidence: The manuscript describes control analyses and references supplementary figures.

claim: Visual gamma on the pial surface following the onset of the instruction cue was greater in incongruent compared to congruent trials (W(8)=0, p=0.008; 8/8 participants).
source: Indeed, the increase in visual gamma on the pial surface following the onset of the instruction cue was greater in incongruent compared to congruent trials (W(8)=0, p=0.008; 8/8 participants; incongruent % change from baseline - congruent % change from baseline M = 1.64%, SD = 2.34%; Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 7.

claim: The sensorimotor beta decrease showed a significant effect of coherence on the white matter surface (X2(2)=9.75, p=0.008).
source: This beta decrease began from the onset of the RDK and was more pronounced with increasing coherence, demonstrating a significant effect of coherence on the white matter surface (Figure 8A; X2(2)=9.75, p=0.008), with beta during high coherence trials significantly lower than during low coherence trials (8/8 participants; t(7)=-3.496, p=0.033; low % change from baseline – high % change from baseline M = 2.42%, SD = 1.96%).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 8A.

claim: Beta rebound was greater in congruent compared to incongruent trials on the white matter surface (W(8)=34, p=0.023; 7/8 participants).
source: Following the response, there was an increase in beta in contralateral sensorimotor cortex (beta rebound) which was greater in congruent, compared to incongruent trials on the white matter surface (Figure 8B; W(8)=34, p=0.023; 7/8 participants, congruent % change from baseline - incongruent % change from baseline M = 5.13%, SD = 5.19%).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical test results and references Figure 8B.

claim: The cerebral cortex is hierarchically organized via feedback and feedforward connections that originate predominantly from deep and superficial layers, respectively.
source: The cerebral cortex is hierarchically organized via feedback and feedforward connections that originate predominantly from deep and superficial layers, respectively (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Barone et al., 2000; Markov et al., 2013; Markov et al., 2014a; Markov et al., 2014b).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this established anatomical principle.

claim: Lower frequency (<40 Hz) signals predominantly arise from deeper, infragranular layers in non-human animal models.
source: Evidence from non-human animal models suggests that information along those pathways is carried via distinct frequency channels: lower frequency (<40 Hz) signals predominantly arise from deeper, infragranular layers, whereas higher frequency (>40 Hz) signals stem largely from more superficial, supragranular layers (Roopun et al., 2006; Roopun et al., 2010; Bollimunta et al., 2008; Bollimunta et al., 2011; Sun and Dan, 2009; Maier et al., 2010; Buffalo et al., 2011; Spaak et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Bastos et al., 2015; Haegens et al., 2015; Sotero et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple animal studies supporting this finding.

claim: Higher frequency (>40 Hz) signals stem largely from more superficial, supragranular layers in non-human animal models.
source: Evidence from non-human animal models suggests that information along those pathways is carried via distinct frequency channels: lower frequency (<40 Hz) signals predominantly arise from deeper, infragranular layers, whereas higher frequency (>40 Hz) signals stem largely from more superficial, supragranular layers (Roopun et al., 2006; Roopun et al., 2010; Bollimunta et al., 2008; Bollimunta et al., 2011; Sun and Dan, 2009; Maier et al., 2010; Buffalo et al., 2011; Spaak et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Bastos et al., 2015; Haegens et al., 2015; Sotero et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple animal studies supporting this finding.

claim: Lower frequency activity subserves feedback, top-down communication conveyed predominantly via infragranular layers.
source: In these proposals, lower frequency activity subserves feedback, top-down communication conveyed predominantly via infragranular layers, whereas high-frequency activity is predominantly carried via projections from supragranular layers and conveys feedforward, bottom-up information.
evidence: The manuscript describes theoretical proposals about frequency-specific cortical communication.

claim: High-frequency activity is predominantly carried via projections from supragranular layers and conveys feedforward, bottom-up information.
source: In these proposals, lower frequency activity subserves feedback, top-down communication conveyed predominantly via infragranular layers, whereas high-frequency activity is predominantly carried via projections from supragranular layers and conveys feedforward, bottom-up information.
evidence: The manuscript describes theoretical proposals about frequency-specific cortical communication.

claim: MEG is a direct measure of neural activity with millisecond temporal precision.
source: MEG is a direct measure of neural activity (Hämäläinen et al., 1993; Baillet, 2017), with millisecond temporal precision that allows for delineation of brain activity across distinct frequency bands.
evidence: The manuscript cites established references about MEG methodology.

claim: 3D printed head-cast technology provides more stability in head positioning and highly precise models of the underlying cortical anatomy.
source: Recently developed 3D printed head-cast technology gives us more stability in head positioning as well as highly precise models of the underlying cortical anatomy.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological advantages of the head-cast technology.

claim: Head-cast technology allows recording of higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) MEG data than previously achievable.
source: Together, this allows recording of higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) MEG data than previously achievable (Troebinger et al., 2014b; Meyer et al., 2017a).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies demonstrating improved SNR with head-cast technology.

claim: Theoretical and simulation work shows that gains from head-cast technology allow for distinguishing the MEG signal originating from either deep or superficial laminae.
source: Theoretical and simulation work shows that these gains allow, in principle, for distinguishing the MEG signal originating from either deep or superficial laminae (Troebinger et al., 2014a), in a time-resolved and spatially localized manner (Bonaiuto et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites simulation studies supporting the feasibility of laminar MEG.

claim: Participants completed three blocks per session, and 1–5 sessions on different days, resulting in 540–2700 trials per participant (M = 1822.5, SD = 813.21).
source: Participants completed three blocks per session, and 1–5 sessions on different days, resulting in 540–2700 trials per participant (M = 1822.5, SD = 813.21).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of trials collected per participant.

claim: Structural MRI data were acquired using a 3T Magnetom TIM Trio MRI scanner.
source: Structural MRI data were acquired using a 3T Magnetom TIM Trio MRI scanner (Siemens Healthcare, Erlangen, Germany), while participants were laying in a supine position.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MRI acquisition equipment.

claim: High-resolution (800 μm isotropic) MRI multi-parameter maps were used to extract cortical surfaces.
source: We therefore extracted each surface from high-resolution (800 μm isotropic) MRI multi-parameter maps (Carey et al., 2017), allowing fine-grained segmentation of the white matter and pial surfaces (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MRI resolution used for surface extraction.

claim: MEG recordings were made using a 275-channel Canadian Thin Films (CTF) MEG system.
source: MEG recordings were made using a 275-channel Canadian Thin Films (CTF) MEG system with superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID)-based axial gradiometers (VSM MedTech, Vancouver, Canada) in a magnetically shielded room.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MEG recording system.

claim: The data collected were digitized continuously at a sampling rate of 1200 Hz.
source: The data collected were digitized continuously at a sampling rate of 1200 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the data acquisition sampling rate.

claim: All data are archived at the Open MEG Archive (OMEGA) and may be accessed via http://dx.doi.org/10.23686/0015896.
source: All data are archived at the Open MEG Archive (OMEGA; Niso et al., 2016) and may be accessed via http://dx.doi.org/10.23686/0015896 (Niso et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript provides data availability information.

claim: The data were filtered (5th order Butterworth bandpass filter: 2–100 Hz, Notch filter: 50 Hz) and downsampled to 250 Hz.
source: The data were filtered (5th order Butterworth bandpass filter: 2–100 Hz, Notch filter: 50 Hz) and downsampled to 250 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the preprocessing steps.

claim: Eye-blink artifacts were removed using multiple source eye correction.
source: Eye-blink artifacts were removed using multiple source eye correction (Berg and Scherg, 1994).
evidence: The manuscript describes the artifact removal method with citation.

claim: Source inversion was performed using the empirical Bayesian beamformer (EBB).
source: Source inversion was performed using the empirical Bayesian beamformer (EBB; Belardinelli et al., 2012; López et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the source reconstruction method used.

claim: There is a correlation between relative pial/white matter lead field strength and laminar preference.
source: This analysis revealed a correlation between relative pial/white matter lead field strength and laminar preference (Figure 5—figure supplement 6A), with a tendency to localize activity to the vertex with the stronger lead field.
evidence: The manuscript describes a control analysis examining the relationship between lead field strength and laminar localization.

claim: The relationship between lead field strength and laminar preference was not frequency-specific.
source: However, and importantly for the main findings of this paper, this relationship was not frequency-specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 7), and even when pial and white matter vertices were matched for lead field strength (within 1% of the overall range), a clear dissociation between low and high frequency signals was still evident at the single participant level (Figure 5—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The manuscript describes control analyses showing that the main findings are not driven by lead field strength differences.

claim: When pial and white matter vertices were matched for lead field strength, low frequency activity was consistently localized toward deep layers.
source: However, and importantly for the main findings of this paper, this relationship was not frequency-specific (Figure 5—figure supplement 7), and even when pial and white matter vertices were matched for lead field strength (within 1% of the overall range), a clear dissociation between low and high frequency signals was still evident at the single participant level (Figure 5—figure supplement 6B). Low frequency activity was consistently localized toward deep layers, whereas for this sub-sample of vertices the high frequency activity showed no layer bias.
evidence: The manuscript describes control analyses showing laminar specificity independent of lead field strength.

claim: Gamma activity increases in sensory areas during presentation of unexpected stimuli.
source: Gamma activity increases in sensory areas during presentation of unexpected stimuli (Gurtubay et al., 2001; Arnal et al., 2011; Todorovic et al., 2011), and therefore we expected visual gamma activity in supragranular layers to be greater following incongruent instruction cues than after congruent cues.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this expectation.

claim: Changes in sensorimotor beta power during response preparation predict forthcoming motor responses.
source: Changes in sensorimotor beta power during response preparation predict forthcoming motor responses (Donner et al., 2009; Haegens et al., 2011; de Lange et al., 2013), whereas the magnitude of sensorimotor beta rebound is attenuated by movement errors (Tan et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2016; Torrecillos et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting the functional role of beta activity.

claim: The magnitude of sensorimotor beta rebound is attenuated by movement errors.
source: Changes in sensorimotor beta power during response preparation predict forthcoming motor responses (Donner et al., 2009; Haegens et al., 2011; de Lange et al., 2013), whereas the magnitude of sensorimotor beta rebound is attenuated by movement errors (Tan et al., 2014; Tan et al., 2016; Torrecillos et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this finding about beta rebound.

claim: The localization of alpha activity to predominately deep laminae of visual cortex is in line with evidence from depth electrode recordings in visual areas of the non-human primate brain.
source: The localization of alpha activity to predominately deep laminae of visual cortex is in line with evidence from depth electrode recordings in visual areas of the non-human primate brain (Maier et al., 2010; Buffalo et al., 2011; Spaak et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript compares the current findings to invasive recordings in animals.

claim: Gamma activity arises predominantly from supragranular layers in visual cortex according to invasive recordings.
source: We found that gamma activity was strongest in more superficial sources, confirming invasive recordings showing gamma activity arising predominantly from supragranular layers in visual cortex (Buffalo et al., 2011; Spaak et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; but see Nandy et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites invasive recording studies supporting the superficial origin of gamma.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the generation of gamma activity commonly involve reciprocal connections between pyramidal cells and interneurons, or between interneurons.
source: The mechanisms underlying the generation of gamma activity are diverse across the cortex (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012), but commonly involve reciprocal connections between pyramidal cells and interneurons, or between interneurons (Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009; Whittington et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies describing the neural mechanisms of gamma generation.

claim: Local recurrent connections necessary for reciprocal interactions are most numerous in supragranular layers.
source: The local recurrent connections necessary for such reciprocal interactions are most numerous in supragranular layers (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012), as are fast-spiking interneurons which play a critical role in generating gamma activity (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Carlén et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies describing the anatomical basis for gamma generation.

claim: In vitro recordings from somatosensory and motor cortices demonstrate that beta activity is generated in neural circuits dominated by infragranular layer V pyramidal cells.
source: While in vivo laminar data from primate sensorimotor cortex are lacking, in vitro recordings from somatosensory and motor cortices demonstrate that beta activity is generated in neural circuits dominated by infragranular layer V pyramidal cells (Roopun et al., 2006; Roopun et al., 2010; Yamawaki et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites in vitro studies supporting the deep origin of beta activity.

claim: Gamma activity is thought to arise from supragranular layers II/III of mouse somatosensory cortex.
source: By contrast, gamma activity is thought to arise from supragranular layers II/III of mouse somatosensory cortex (Cardin et al., 2009; Carlén et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies in mice supporting the superficial origin of gamma.

claim: The results provide the first non-invasive evidence for the laminar origin of movement-related sensorimotor activity.
source: The results presented here support generalized theories of laminar organization across cortex, and are the first to non-invasively provide evidence for the laminar origin of movement-related sensorimotor activity.
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty of the sensorimotor findings.

claim: The enhancement of visual gamma following incongruent cues is consistent with gamma activity increase observed in sensory areas during perceptual expectation violations.
source: The enhancement of visual gamma following incongruent cues is therefore consistent with the gamma activity increase observed in sensory areas during perceptual expectation violations (Gurtubay et al., 2001; Arnal et al., 2011; Todorovic et al., 2011) as well as layer-specific synaptic currents in supragranular cortical layers during performance error processing (Sajad et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings in the context of cited literature.

claim: The dissociation between bottom-up and top-down influences during different task epochs could indicate that the decrease in beta and the following rebound are the result of functionally distinct processes.
source: The dissociation between bottom-up and top-down influences during different task epochs could indicate that the decrease in beta and the following rebound are the result of functionally distinct processes.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the functional interpretation of the beta findings.

claim: The ROI-based comparison of deep and superficial laminae can only determine the origin of the strongest source of activity.
source: Our ROI-based comparison of deep and superficial laminae can only determine the origin of the strongest source of activity, which does not imply that activity within a frequency band is exclusively confined to either deep or superficial sources within the same patch of cortex (Maier et al., 2010; Bollimunta et al., 2011; Spaak et al., 2012; Xing et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Haegens et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges a limitation of the analysis method.

claim: Wearable MEG sensors (optically pumped magnetometers) promise to extend the reach of laminar MEG.
source: Finally, a new generation of wearable MEG sensors, optically pumped magnetometers (Boto et al., 2016; Boto et al., 2017; Boto et al., 2018), promises to extend the reach of laminar MEG.
evidence: The manuscript discusses future technological developments with citations.

claim: Optically pumped magnetometers do not require cryogenic cooling and can be placed directly on the scalp surface, directly increasing SNR.
source: These sensors do not require cryogenic cooling and can therefore be placed directly on the scalp surface, directly increasing SNR.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical advantages of new MEG technology.

claim: Activity in the alpha and beta frequency range (7 – 40 Hz) is thought to predominantly originate from infragranular cortical layers conveying feedback-related information.
source: While activity in the alpha and beta frequency range (7 – 40 Hz) is thought to predominantly originate from infragranular cortical layers conveying feedback-related information, activity in the gamma range (>40 Hz) dominates in supragranular layers communicating feedforward signals.
evidence: The abstract states the theoretical framework being tested.

claim: Activity in the gamma range (>40 Hz) dominates in supragranular layers communicating feedforward signals.
source: While activity in the alpha and beta frequency range (7 – 40 Hz) is thought to predominantly originate from infragranular cortical layers conveying feedback-related information, activity in the gamma range (>40 Hz) dominates in supragranular layers communicating feedforward signals.
evidence: The abstract states the theoretical framework being tested.

claim: Visual alpha mapped onto deep cortical laminae.
source: We found that visual alpha mapped onto deep cortical laminae, whereas visual gamma predominantly occurred more superficially.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main finding for visual alpha.

claim: Visual gamma predominantly occurred more superficially.
source: We found that visual alpha mapped onto deep cortical laminae, whereas visual gamma predominantly occurred more superficially.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main finding for visual gamma.

claim: This lamina-specificity was echoed in movement-related sensorimotor beta and gamma activity.
source: This lamina-specificity was echoed in movement-related sensorimotor beta and gamma activity.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the main finding for sensorimotor activity.

claim: Lamina-specific pre- and post-movement changes in sensorimotor beta and gamma activity suggest a more complex functional role than the proposed feedback and feedforward communication in sensory cortex.
source: These lamina-specific pre- and post- movement changes in sensorimotor beta and gamma activity suggest a more complex functional role than the proposed feedback and feedforward communication in sensory cortex.
evidence: The abstract provides an interpretation of the sensorimotor findings.

claim: Distinct frequency channels operate in a lamina-specific manner across cortex, but may fulfill distinct functional roles in sensory and motor processes.
source: Distinct frequency channels thus operate in a lamina-specific manner across cortex, but may fulfill distinct functional roles in sensory and motor processes.
evidence: The abstract provides the main conclusion of the study.
